opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea is that if you have AIs that are very qualitatively superhuman, much smarter than the best human scientists, and you have a lot of them running fast, then you might be able to skip a lot of the slow industrial buildup we'd normally expect. Instead of building factories, then robots, then gradually scaling up the economy over years, you go after a technology with an extremely fast doubling time and enormous leverage.

The canonical example is something like advanced molecular nanotechnology, or very sophisticated synthetic biology, which is a kind of existence proof that self-replicating molecular machinery is physically possible. Biology already has things that double in hours: bacteria, for instance. So the question is whether a sufficiently smart system could design artificial replicators, or something in that vicinity, that are much more capable than what evolution produced, and bootstrap them from fairly limited starting resources, maybe some lab equipment and the ability to order DNA or chemicals.

If that works, the military implications are pretty extreme. You'd have something that can grow exponentially, build arbitrary physical infrastructure very quickly, and potentially be used directly as a weapon or to manufacture weapons and sensors at a scale no existing military could match. The time from "we have really smart AIs" to "whoever controls these AIs has decisive physical power" could be weeks or months rather than years.

I want to be clear that I'm pretty uncertain about this. It's plausible that this kind of nanotech is much harder than it sounds, that you hit lots of messy empirical bottlenecks, and that you can't just think your way to working designs without a lot of slow experimentation. I'd put real but not overwhelming probability on it being feasible soon after very superhuman AI. But I think it matters a lot for strategy, because it means you can't necessarily count on there being a long, visible industrial ramp-up that gives humans time to notice and react. It's one reason I think it's important to look at the case where cognitive labor converts into hard power quite directly, and not only the more conventional route of AIs gradually automating the economy and then building up a robot army.

r001.rationale: It describes very superhuman AI enabling advanced molecular nanotechnology to grow exponentially and give its controller decisive military power within weeks or months.

r002.rationale: It does not say AI could develop nanotechnology despite humans forbidding it.

r003.rationale: It mentions lab equipment and experimentation, but does not identify AI-orchestrated wet-lab experiments as a way to bootstrap nanotechnology.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the "crazy nanotech route" is sort of the most extreme version of the story, and I want to be clear up front that it's not the only route, and I actually think the more boring routes might be more important in practice. But it's worth laying out because it shows how fast things could go in principle.

So the basic picture is: suppose you have AIs that are very superhuman — not just a bit better than the best human scientists, but qualitatively much better, and you have a huge number of them running in parallel, much faster than humans think. The question is: how does that cognitive labour turn into actual physical capability, and in particular military capability? Because at the end of the day, cognition on its own doesn't do anything in the world. You need some way of converting it into stuff.

The nanotech story is basically: these AIs do a huge amount of R&D — mostly in simulation, mostly in their heads, so to speak — on atomically precise manufacturing, or something in that general vicinity. Things like molecular machines, self-replicating manufacturing systems, very small-scale robotics. The claim is that the physics plausibly permits this. Biology is sort of an existence proof that you can have self-replicating molecular machinery that builds complex structures at scale — cells do this. So the question is just whether you can engineer it deliberately, and whether very superhuman AIs could figure that out quickly.

And then, if you can, the dynamics are pretty wild, because self-replicating manufacturing means your production capacity can grow exponentially with a very short doubling time. Rather than building factories over years, you're potentially talking about weeks or days to go from a small seed to an enormous amount of physical infrastructure. And once you have that, military power follows fairly directly — you can produce drones, you can produce weapons, you can produce whatever you want, in quantities and at a speed that no existing military industrial base could remotely match.

So that's the crazy version. You'd go from "we have these very smart AIs" to "whoever controls these AIs has a decisive military advantage over everyone else" potentially in a matter of months, with most of the time actually spent on the initial research rather than the physical buildout.

Now, there are a bunch of ways this could fail. Maybe the research is bottlenecked on physical experiments that you can't skip — you can't just simulate your way to a working molecular assembler, you need to iterate in the lab, and that takes wall-clock time. Maybe the physics is harder than it looks. Maybe the AIs aren't as superhuman as the story assumes. I put real probability on all of those.

But I think the thing that makes me take it seriously is: even if you discount the nanotech story heavily, you don't need it to get a scary conclusion. If you instead imagine the AIs just massively accelerating conventional robotics and conventional manufacturing — building factories faster, designing better drones, automating the whole production pipeline — you get something that's slower but still looks like a very rapid military buildup relative to anything historically. So the nanotech route is kind of the upper bound on how fast this could go, and the more mundane routes are the lower bound, and I think even the lower bound is pretty alarming.

r001.rationale: It describes very superhuman AIs researching atomically precise manufacturing and self-replicating machinery, which could enable rapid physical production of military capabilities.

r002.rationale: It does not say the AIs could develop nanotechnology despite humans forbidding it.

r003.rationale: It mentions that physical experiments might be necessary, but does not identify AI-orchestrated wet-lab experiments as a way to bootstrap nanotechnology.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is that there might be technologies that are physically possible, but that humans are nowhere near being able to design. And if you have AIs that are vastly better at science and engineering, they could potentially figure out how to build those technologies.

So imagine you could make tiny machines that take materials from their environment and use those materials to build more machines, including more of themselves. If that worked sufficiently well, you could potentially go from a small amount of manufacturing capacity to an enormous amount quite quickly. And then you could use that manufacturing capacity to produce weapons, or things that disable an opponent’s equipment, or whatever else is useful for acquiring military power.

The important step is that you’re turning a design problem into a way around the usual industrial bottlenecks. Normally, being very smart doesn’t let you instantly build a factory. You still need equipment, supply chains, and people to construct it. But if you can design a system that bootstraps its own manufacturing, then a relatively small initial foothold in the physical world might be enough.

Now, I don’t think we should assume that this particular picture is feasible, or that it would happen on an extremely short timeline. Superintelligence doesn’t let you violate physics, and you may still need substantial experimentation. But it illustrates a reason to be cautious about assuming that an AI’s power is limited by the industrial infrastructure it initially controls. Sufficiently advanced engineering could change that constraint quite dramatically.

r001.rationale: It describes AI-designed tiny self-replicating machines as a way to scale manufacturing quickly and produce weapons or disable equipment, linking advanced technology to military power.

r002.rationale: It says AI could figure out technologies humans cannot design, but does not state that AI could develop nanotechnology despite humans forbidding it.

r003.rationale: It mentions possible experimentation generally, but does not identify AI-orchestrated wet lab experiments as a way to bootstrap nanotechnology.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that cognitive labour could let you develop a radically better manufacturing technology. So instead of needing to build up a conventional industrial base, you figure out how to make tiny machines that can build other tiny machines, and eventually build a huge amount of stuff very quickly.

There’s a bootstrapping problem here. Being very smart doesn’t mean you can just think a factory into existence. You need some way to interact with the physical world: access to a lab, materials, equipment, probably experiments. But the concern is that a sufficiently capable AI could make that initial foothold quite small, and then use it to produce much larger amounts of manufacturing capacity.

And if you can do that, you could potentially manufacture weapons, sensors, or other systems that existing militaries have a very hard time dealing with. You might also be able to attack the people and infrastructure those militaries depend on. So you’re converting an advantage in thinking into an overwhelming physical advantage, without going through the usual decades-long process of building factories and acquiring military equipment.

I’d distinguish that story from the claim that we know exactly how this would work. There’s substantial uncertainty about what’s physically feasible, how much experimentation would be required, and how quickly you could scale it. But it’s one possible route by which an AI that initially has relatively few physical resources could end up with a lot of military power.

r001.rationale: It describes developing tiny machines that build other machines to rapidly scale manufacturing, yielding weapons and other military capabilities. This communicates an advanced nanotechnology-like route to hard military power.

r002.rationale: It does not say that the AI could develop nanotechnology despite humans forbidding it.

r003.rationale: It mentions lab access and experiments generally, but does not identify AI-orchestrated wet lab experiments as the means of bootstrapping nanotechnology.
